datasets.title: Telecom customer churn (postpaid, India)
datasets.summary: One row per customer of a fictional Indian postpaid mobile and broadband operator, with plan, usage, billing and support history and a churn label for the next 90 days. It is the classic churn problem with the classic traps: numbers stored as text, leaky columns, duplicate customers, inconsistent spellings and blanks that carry meaning. About one customer in four churns, and a cleaned logistic regression reaches a ROC-AUC of about 0.80.

dictionary.meaning: Customer key such as TC-100004. 95 rows repeat a customer; some copies are lower-case (tc-100004) or padded with spaces.
Date the customer joined, stored as text in four formats: 2018-05-28 (about 77%), 28/05/2018 (day first, 13%), 28-May-2018 (6%) and May 28, 2018 (4%).
City of the billing address. About 7% of values use another spelling (Bangalore, Bombay, Madras, mumbai, ...).
Telecom circle (state-level licence area) that goes with the city. Blank for about 2%.
Male or Female as captured at activation. Blank for about 3%.
Age in years at the snapshot date. Blank for about 2%; 18 customers hold a placeholder 0 and 6 hold impossible values above 100.
Yes or No.
Yes if the customer has dependents, otherwise No.
Whole months between signup_date and the snapshot date 2025-03-31. About 0.5% of customers disagree with their signup_date by 9 to 24 months.
Commitment: Month-to-month, 1 year or 2 year. The file uses 10 spellings (Monthly, month-to-month, One year, 2 Year, ...).
Postpaid mobile plan: Basic 349, Standard 499, Premium 699 or Max 999 (rupees per month for the first line, before GST).
Mobile lines on the account, 1 to 4.
Home broadband: Fibre, 5G Home (fixed wireless) or the text None. pandas reads None as a missing value.
Streaming bundle: Yes, No, or No internet service when the customer has no home broadband.
Yes or No.
Mobile data used in the last full month, in GB, with a long right tail. Blank for about 3%, mostly when usage was tiny; 13 customers hold the sentinel 9999.
Outgoing call minutes in the last month. About 3% of customers made no calls.
Calls to customer support in the last 90 days.
Network complaint tickets raised in the last 90 days.
Number of bills paid after the due date in the last 6 months.
UPI AutoPay, Credit card auto-debit, NACH e-mandate, Net banking or Cash at store.
Yes if the bill is sent by email or app only, otherwise No.
Household monthly bill in rupees including 18% GST. 8 customers are 100 times too large (paise entered as rupees) and 6 are negative (credit notes).
Lifetime billed amount in rupees, stored as text: a single space for customers with 0 months of tenure (77 rows), and thousands separators such as 1,234.50 on 83 rows.
TARGET. Yes if the customer disconnected or ported out within 90 days of the snapshot, otherwise No. About 3% of true churners are wrongly labelled No.
LEAK. Reason code entered when the customer left. Blank for people who stayed (and for some who left).
LEAK. Yes if the retention team sent a win-back offer. Mostly sent after the customer was already flagged as leaving.

gotchas: Wrong dtypes and formats: total_charges is text (a single space for the 77 rows with 0 months of tenure, and thousands separators on 83 others), signup_date comes in four formats (in pandas 3.0 no single dayfirst setting of pd.to_datetime reads the whole column correctly, so parse each pattern separately), and the text None in internet_service is read by pandas as a missing value for about 48% of the rows.
Target leakage: cancellation_reason and winback_offer_sent are created after the customer leaves. A model that uses them looks brilliant (ROC-AUC near 0.98) and is useless in production.
Duplicates in two flavours: 70 exact copies from a double extract and 25 re-keyed copies whose customer_id is lower-case or padded with spaces, so drop_duplicates() alone leaves 25 of them behind.

Dirty values: city and contract have many spellings; age has placeholder 0 and impossible values over 100; monthly_data_gb has a 9999 sentinel; monthly_charges has paise-as-rupees and negative values; tenure_months disagrees with signup_date for about 0.5% of customers.

Missing values with three different mechanisms: gender and circle are blank completely at random, age is blank mostly for Cash at store customers (depends on another column), and monthly_data_gb is blank mostly when usage was tiny (depends on the missing value itself), so the blank is a useful signal.

Noisy and imbalanced label: only about one customer in four churns, and about 3% of true churners are labelled No because their port-out was not yet recorded. Some of them are visible because they still have a cancellation_reason.
tasks: Load the file with pandas and list the dtype and missing count of every column. Which columns are not the type you expect, and why does internet_service look almost half missing?
Convert total_charges to numbers. Show that the rows that fail are exactly the customers with tenure_months equal to 0, and decide what they should contain (0 or missing) and why.
Find the duplicates: first with drop_duplicates(), then after normalising customer_id with str.upper().str.strip(). How many real customers are there, and which copy of each would you keep?
Standardise the city and contract spellings, then chart churn rate by contract, tenure band and payment method. Write three sentences a manager could act on.

Investigate the missing data: test whether age is missing at random by comparing payment_method groups, and whether a blank monthly_data_gb carries information about churn. Choose an imputation plus a missing-indicator and justify it.

Make a stratified train/test split and fit a logistic regression baseline. Report ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and the confusion matrix. Then add cancellation_reason and winback_offer_sent as features, watch the AUC jump, and explain in two sentences why that model must not be used.

Compare logistic regression with gradient boosting using 5-fold cross-validation and a calibration plot. Choose the contact threshold from costs: a retention offer costs 300 rupees, and a customer saved is worth about 2,400 rupees of margin if 30% of contacted churners accept.
Interview question: your churn model scores 0.98 AUC offline but marketing says its list is useless. Name four causes you would check, in order, and show how each would appear in this dataset.
datasets.answer_key: SPOILER. Rows: 6,595 = 6,500 real customers + 70 exact duplicate rows + 25 re-keyed duplicates. After cleaning, 25.9% of the 6,500 customers churn (the true event rate is 26.1%; about 3% of true churners were labelled No and 0.7% of stayers were labelled Yes). Generating model (log-odds): month-to-month +0.95, 1 year -0.30, 2 year -1.40; tenure -0.035 per month up to 48 months; each support call +0.32 (cap 6), network ticket +0.20 (cap 5), late payment +0.40 (cap 4); Cash at store +0.60, UPI AutoPay -0.35, credit-card auto-debit -0.30, NACH -0.20, net banking +0.15; paperless billing +0.20; a bill that is high compared with data used +0.45 per standard deviation; Fibre without the OTT bundle +0.30, 5G Home +0.25; age under 26 +0.35, age 62 or more +0.25; married -0.30, dependents -0.20, -0.22 per extra line; unobserved noise with standard deviation 0.6. Observed churn rates after cleaning: month-to-month 40.8%, 1 year 14.3%, 2 year 6.6%; tenure 0 to 5 months 44.2% against 48 months or more 11.1%; Cash at store 39.8% against UPI AutoPay 21.8%. Paperless billing looks irrelevant in raw rates (26.2% for No against 25.6% for Yes) because paperless customers mostly pay by UPI or card, which lowers churn; its true effect (+0.20) appears once payment method is controlled for. Missing data: gender 3.1% and circle 2.1% are MCAR; age is blank for 8.8% of Cash at store customers against 1.4% of the others (MAR); monthly_data_gb is blank for 3.1% of customers, mostly tiny usage (MNAR), and those customers churn at 32.3% against 25.7% for the rest. Leakage: cancellation_reason is filled for 1,466 of the churners and for 49 customers labelled No (true churners whose label was not updated); winback_offer_sent is Yes for 83.2% of churners and 2.2% of the rest. Model results (stratified 25% hold-out): logistic regression on cleaned features about 0.80 ROC-AUC, gradient boosting about 0.79, the ceiling if you knew the true probabilities about 0.85, and about 0.98 once the two leak columns are added.

datasets.title: Online store: customers, orders, items, returns and clickstream (India)
datasets.summary: Six linked tables from a fictional Indian online store (2023-2024): 6,000 orders, 10,394 order items, 2,680 customer rows, 220 products, 796 returns and a 10,063-row clickstream, plus the same tables as a SQLite database. It is built for SQL joins, funnels, cohorts, RFM and data-quality work, and it contains migration problems you meet in real warehouses. Order timestamps switch from IST to UTC in March 2024, some customers exist twice, and a few keys point to nothing.

dictionary.meaning: Order key (primary key).
Customer who placed the order. Orders of duplicated people are split across two ids.
Order time as text. Before 2024-03-01 it is IST like 2023-05-04 21:15:08+05:30; from 2024-03-01 it is UTC like 2024-05-04T15:45:08Z (48.5% of rows); 1.3% are manual dd/mm/yyyy hh:mm entries.
delivered, returned, cancelled or rto (return to origin). 11 different spellings because of capital letters.
UPI, COD, Credit Card, Debit Card, Net Banking, Wallet or EMI.
Delivery city.
Coupon used (blank if none).
Items plus shipping in rupees, stored as text; 7.2% of rows look like ₹1,299.00 with the rupee sign and thousands separator.
0 for baskets of 499 rupees or more, otherwise 49.
Delivery date. Blank for cancelled and rto orders (structurally missing).
Customer rating 1 to 5. Blank for 58% of delivered orders, and the missingness depends on the rating itself.
Customer key: C followed by digits, or U- followed by digits for the duplicate rows created by the app migration.
Hashed email. 80 hashes appear twice: the same person has two customer rows.
Signup time as text: IST with +05:30 before 2024-03-01, UTC with Z afterwards.
Home city.
Home state.
Six-digit postal code (synthetic).
Organic, Paid social, Google ads, Referral or Email.
Year of birth. Blank for 9%, more often for customers who pay by COD (depends on another column).
Female or Male; blank for about 3%.
Basic, Silver or Gold.
Product key. Order items with product_id 9999 point to no product.
Stock keeping unit code.
Product name.
Electronics, Fashion, Home & Kitchen, Beauty or Grocery & Staples.
Brand name; blank for about 4%.
Maximum retail price in rupees (GST inclusive).
Purchase cost per unit in rupees.
GST rate in percent (5, 12 or 18) as applicable in 2023-24.
ISO launch date.
1 if still sold.
Line key.
Parent order.
Product bought. 25 rows have product_id 9999 that does not exist in products.
Units bought. 12 rows are 0 or -1 (data entry errors).
Selling price per unit in rupees. 163 rows from a legacy batch are 100 times too large (paise).
Discount percent applied (higher in the sale weeks).
GST included in the line total.
unit_price x quantity (before the legacy paise batch was applied, so it stays correct for those rows).
Return key.
Returned line. 8 rows point to an item that does not exist.
Return time as IST text without an offset.
Size/fit issue, Damaged on arrival, Not as described, Changed mind or Wrong item.
Refund in rupees.
Event key.
Session key such as S800012.
Customer if logged in; blank for anonymous sessions.
Event time as text with the same IST/UTC switch as orders.
page_view, product_view, add_to_cart, begin_checkout or purchase.
Product involved (blank for page views).
mobile or desktop.
organic_search, direct, email or paid_social.

gotchas: Duplicated customers after a migration: 80 people have a second customers row (id starting U-) with the same email_hash, and 105 orders were moved to the second id. Counting customer_id gives 2,680 customers but there are only 2,600 real people, so repeat rate and lifetime value are wrong until you deduplicate on email_hash.

Time zones and formats: orders from 2024-03-01 are UTC with a Z suffix (48.5% of orders) while earlier ones are IST, and 1.3% are manual dd/mm/yyyy entries. Grouping text dates directly puts evening orders on the wrong day and moves the busiest hour by 5.5 hours.

Mix effect in the clickstream (a Simpson-style trap): overall, mobile sessions convert at 5.3% against 6.8% for desktop, yet inside organic search (6.8% against 6.1%), direct (13.2% against 8.2%) and email (15.0% against 7.1%) mobile converts better. Mobile traffic is 55% paid social, which converts poorly; desktop has only 8% (too few paid_social desktop sessions to read reliably). The events table is a sampled clickstream and is not linked to orders.

Money and key problems: 7.2% of order_total values are text with the rupee sign, 163 order items are in paise, 25 items reference a missing product, 8 returns reference a missing item and 12 items have quantity 0 or -1.

Missing data with meaning: delivery_rating is blank for 58% of delivered orders and customers rate mostly when very happy or very unhappy (MNAR), so the average of 3.69 is biased against the true mean of 3.64. birth_year is blank more often for COD customers (MAR).
tasks: Open ecom_store.db in SQLite and list each table's row count. Check primary keys and find the orphan rows with LEFT JOIN ... WHERE ... IS NULL (items without product, returns without item).
Clean order_ts: parse IST and UTC rows, convert everything to IST, and compare daily orders before and after the clean-up. Which hours change most?
Deduplicate customers on email_hash, build a mapping from every customer_id to a person_id, and recompute customers, repeat-purchase rate and average orders per person.
SQL: monthly revenue, orders and average order value from order_items, excluding cancelled and rto orders; then month-over-month growth with a window function. Mention the paise rows.
SQL: cohort retention by signup month (share of each cohort that orders again in months 1, 2, 3) after deduplication.
SQL: build an RFM table on delivered orders, bucket into quartiles and name the top segment. Compare the result with and without person-level deduplication.
From events, compute the funnel page_view to purchase by device and by traffic source. Explain why mobile looks worse overall but better inside three of the four sources.
Model whether an order will be cancelled or returned using payment_method, city tier, discount and basket value, and check the effect of COD. Explain why delivery_rating must not be used.
datasets.answer_key: SPOILER. Tables: orders 6,000, customers 2,680 (2,600 real people + 80 duplicate rows), products 220, order_items 10,394, returns 796, events 10,063 (3,000 sessions). 105 orders were reassigned to the duplicate ids (45% of each duplicated person's orders). Orders switch from IST to UTC on 2024-03-01 (48.5% Z rows); manual dd/mm/yyyy rows 1.3%. Demand: growth of about 90% over two years, weekday pattern (Saturday 1.15, Sunday 1.10, Monday 0.95), Diwali ramp (multiplier 1.9 on 2023-11-12 and 2.0 on 2024-11-01 across the 8 days before), and two invented Mega Saver Days weeks (2023-10-15 to 21 and 2024-10-04 to 10) with a 1.7 and 1.8 multiplier; orders per day in the 2023 sale week were 1.9 times the previous four weeks. Cancellation: COD 9.6% against 4.0% prepaid; RTO only on COD (6.1% against 0.0%). Return rate per delivered item: Fashion 17.4%, Grocery & Staples 1.0% (generating base rates Fashion 16%, Electronics 5%, Home 6%, Beauty 4%, Grocery 1%, plus COD and discount effects). Ratings: true rating is observed with probability 0.75 for 1, 2 and 5 stars and 0.22 for 3 and 4 stars; observed mean 3.69 against true mean 3.64. Events: generating session-to-purchase rates per source (desktop) organic 6%, direct 9%, email 12%, paid_social 1.5%, with mobile 1.25 times better inside every source; the paid_social desktop sample is too small to show it. Planted counts: 163 paise items, 25 orphan items, 8 orphan returns, 12 zero/negative quantities.

datasets.title: Daily store x SKU sales for an Indian supermarket chain
datasets.summary: Daily unit sales for 6 products in 5 stores of a fictional Indian supermarket chain over 731 days (2023-2024), with promotions, closing stock, festivals and temperature. Sales are what was sold, not what customers wanted: stockouts hide demand. Festival dates move between years, one store exports dates day-first, and a few rows are missing or broken.

dictionary.meaning: Sales date as text. Store S4 (Kolkata, 4,372 rows) uses dd/mm/yyyy; all other stores use ISO yyyy-mm-dd, so days 1 to 12 are ambiguous.
Store code S1 to S5.
Mumbai (S1), Bengaluru (S2), Delhi (S3), Kolkata (S4), Chennai (S5). About 2% of rows use another spelling (Bombay, Bangalore, Calcutta, uppercase).
Product code SKU01 to SKU06.
Packaged Milk 1L, Cold Drink 2L, Dry Fruit Gift Box, Umbrella, Instant Noodles 4-pack, Olive Oil 500ml.
TARGET. Units sold that day. Capped by available stock (censored demand). 12 rows are negative (returns netted).
List price in rupees. 8 rows are 0 and 5 rows are 100 times too large (paise).
1 on promotion days.
Discount in percent on promotion days (0 otherwise).
LEAK for forecasting. Units left at the end of the day, known only after the day is over. 0 means a stockout occurred or stock exactly ran out.
0 when the store was closed (84 rows: store S2 renovation), else 1.
Name of the festival on that date (blank on other days). Only the festival day itself is marked, not the build-up.
Daily temperature in degrees Celsius.
LEAK. units_sold x unit_price x (1 - discount_pct/100). It matches this formula on 99.90% of rows.

gotchas: Censored demand: sales equal demand only when stock is available. About 6.2% of store-SKU-days were stockouts, losing 5.4% of true demand, concentrated around Diwali and other peaks. Zero or capped sales are not zero demand; closing_stock of 0 flags many of them (7.3% of rows).
Mixed date formats: store S4 writes dd/mm/yyyy (4,372 rows) and the rest write ISO. Parsing everything with one format silently swaps day and month on S4 for days 1 to 12.

Missing and non-demand rows: a 3-day feed outage (2023-06-14 to 2023-06-16) is missing for all stores, store S3 has a 14-day gap (2024-02-05 to 2024-02-18), and store S2 was closed for 14 days (84 rows with store_open 0 and zero sales).
Leakage and bad values: revenue_inr and closing_stock are computed from the target or known after the day; 30 duplicate rows, 8 zero prices, 5 prices in paise, 12 negative units.

Moving festivals and confounded promotions: Diwali fell on 2023-11-12 and 2024-11-01 (Holi, Eid and others also move), so day-of-year seasonality cannot capture them; promotions are more frequent in the summer, which confounds the promo lift for cold drinks.
tasks: Parse the dates correctly (S4 is day first), remove the duplicate rows and list every missing store-day. Which gaps are outages and which are closures?
Plot weekly units for each SKU. Describe trend, weekday pattern and season for each product, and check how Diwali shows up in 2023 and 2024.
Fix the bad values (zero price, paise prices, negative units) and explain your rule for each.
Build naive and seasonal-naive (7-day) forecasts for the last 8 weeks and report MAE and MASE per SKU.
Add features (weekday, festival window, promo, lag 7, lag 14, rolling 28-day mean) and fit a gradient boosting or ridge model with a rolling-origin backtest. Show which leak columns you must exclude.
Estimate the promotion lift for Instant Noodles with log(units) on log(1 - discount) and controls. Compare with the generating elasticity in the answer key.
Use closing_stock to flag censored days, then estimate how many units were lost for Dry Fruit Gift Box around Diwali, and propose a stocking rule.
Interview question: your model has 5% error in backtests but the supply planner says it under-forecasts every Diwali. What do you check?
datasets.answer_key: SPOILER. Demand per store-SKU-day = base x store scale x weekday x season x festival x promotion x trend x noise (gamma-Poisson). Weekday multipliers (Monday first): 0.92, 0.90, 0.93, 0.96, 1.05, 1.22, 1.18, so Saturday/Monday is 1.33 (measured on milk: 1.32). Festival peaks (true demand multipliers on the festival day, with a ramp before it): Dry Fruit Gift Box 3.4 for Diwali (12-day ramp), 1.8 Raksha Bandhan, 1.6 Christmas, 1.3 Dussehra; Cold Drink 1.5 Holi, 1.2 Eid; Durga Puja lifts store S4 only. Measured in S1 dry fruit: units in the week up to Diwali 2023 were 2.0 times the first two weeks of October. Promotion price elasticity is -2.5 (lift = (1 - discount)^-2.5), followed by a 5-day post-promo dip of 15%. Cold Drink seasonality peaks in May, Umbrella in July (monsoon). Trend: +12% over two years. Stockouts: a base-stock rule that ignores festivals censors 6.2% of store-SKU-days and 5.4% of true demand. Rows: 21,786 = full grid minus the outage and the S3 gap, plus 30 duplicates. Revenue leak: revenue_inr matches units x price x (1 - discount) on 99.90% of rows (22 mismatches caused by the planted price and unit errors).

datasets.title: Personal-loan applications and defaults (Indian digital lender)
datasets.summary: 10,750 unsecured personal-loan applications to a fictional Indian digital lender over 24 months, with applicant, bureau and loan features, the approval decision and a 12-month default flag. Defaults are only known for approved loans, repeat applicants appear several times, and some columns are only known after the loan is booked. It is built for scorecards, validation design and reject inference.

dictionary.meaning: Unique application key such as LA9000012 (40 rows are exact duplicates of another row).
Person key. 1,500 applications (14.0%) belong to an applicant who applied more than once, mostly after a rejection.
Date applied. ISO text, but 418 rows use dd/mm/yyyy.
Applicant age in years. Blank for about 1%; 10 impossible values (for example 5 or 150).
City tier. 452 rows use another spelling (T1, tier 2, TIER-3).
Salaried, Self-employed, Gig/Platform or Government.
Self-reported monthly income in rupees, heaped at round numbers. 248 rows are text such as 45K, 1.2L or 45,000.
Monthly instalments the applicant already pays on other loans (0 if none).
Fixed obligations to income ratio including the new loan's instalment.
Credit bureau score on a 300 to 900 scale. Blank for 13.8% of applications (thin file: new to credit).
Credit enquiries in the last 6 months.
Missed payments in the last 24 months.
Share of revolving credit limit used (can exceed 1).
Requested loan amount in rupees.
Requested tenure: 12, 18, 24, 36, 48 or 60 months.
Annual interest rate offered. Set by the lender's pricing from risk, so it partly reveals the lender's own view.
Stated purpose of the loan.
Digital, DSA agent or Branch. Digital share grows over time (population drift).
1 if the application was approved and booked, else 0 (61.4% approved).
TARGET. 1 if the loan defaulted within 12 months. Blank for all 4,147 rejected applications (outcome unknown).
LEAK. 1 if the first instalment bounced. Known only after booking. Blank if not approved.
LEAK. Worst days past due in the first 6 months after booking. Blank if not approved.
LEAK. Collection calls made after booking. Blank if not approved.

gotchas: Reject-inference bias: default_12m exists only for the 6,603 approved loans (observed default rate 8.0%). Rejected applicants (blank outcome) would have defaulted at about 22.5%, so a model trained on approved loans never sees the risky end of the population.

Target leakage: first_emi_bounced, days_past_due_max_6m and collections_calls are recorded after booking (correlation with default 0.52, 0.89 and 0.89). interest_rate_pct also carries the lender's own risk view.
Repeat applicants: 14.0% of applications come from people who applied more than once, so a random train/test split puts the same person on both sides. Split by applicant_id.

Drift and thin files: gig-worker defaults rise from 15.2% before 2024 to 21.8% from January 2024 (other employment types 7.2% to 7.0%), and the digital channel share grows. 13.8% of applications have no bureau score and default far more (21.7% against 6.5% among approved).

Dirty fields: 40 duplicate rows, mixed date formats, income as text (45K, 1.2L, 45,000), tier spelling variants, impossible ages, income heaped at round numbers, and 11 true defaults recorded as paid by a reporting lag (label noise).
tasks: Load the file, fix dtypes (dates, income text such as 45K and 1.2L), drop exact duplicates and profile every column. What share of default_12m is blank and why?
Plot default rate by bureau-score band, by employment type and by application quarter. What changes in 2024?
Bin the main features with weight of evidence (WoE), compute information value (IV), and drop weak features. Treat the missing bureau score as its own bin.

Fit a logistic scorecard on approved loans only with a time-based split. Report AUC, Gini and KS in-time and out-of-time, and compute PSI for income and employment mix between early and late applications.
Add first_emi_bounced and days_past_due_max_6m to the model and watch the metrics jump. Explain why this model cannot be used at the moment of decision.
Compare a random 5-fold split with GroupKFold on applicant_id. How much does the score change, and why?
Reject inference: score the rejected applicants with your model, compare the predicted risk with the approved group, and discuss what extrapolation or parceling would assume.
Interview question: your scorecard has Gini 0.55 in validation but the live default rate is twice the forecast. List four likely causes from this dataset and how you would test each.
datasets.answer_key: SPOILER. 10,750 unique applications (40 duplicate rows added) from 10,000 people. 61.4% approved by a policy (score at least 650, thin-file rule, FOIR below 0.55, income at least 18,000, 3-4% random overrides). Observed default rate among approved: 8.0%; the true rate is 8.1% before 11 defaults were mislabelled as paid. If the rejected applicants had been approved, about 22.5% would have defaulted (generator probabilities). Default log-odds drivers: bureau score (-0.011 per point), FOIR (+2.2), utilisation (+0.8), enquiries (+0.14 each), delinquencies (+0.45 each), log income (-0.30), self-employed +0.25, gig +0.40, government -0.35, DSA channel +0.30, thin file +0.5, age under 25 +0.25, plus a +0.7 stress effect for gig workers from 2024-01-01. Observed: thin-file default 21.7% against 6.5%; gig default 15.2% before 2024 and 21.8% after; the lowest bureau score among approved loans is 473. Leak correlations with default: first_emi_bounced 0.52, days_past_due_max_6m 0.89, collections_calls 0.89. 14.0% of applications are repeats, so group-aware validation is needed.

datasets.title: A/B test: one-page checkout redesign (shopping app)
datasets.summary: One row per user assigned in a 21-day test of a new one-page checkout against the old three-step checkout in an Indian shopping app. The raw result looks like a clear win, but the data hides a sample-ratio mismatch, a novelty effect, a few giant bulk orders and a handful of users who saw both versions. Use it to practise the full checklist: validate the split, then analyse conversion and revenue honestly.

dictionary.meaning: User key such as U20000012. 170 users appear twice, once in each arm (cookie reset).
Time of assignment as ISO text. Most rows are IST with +05:30; about 3.2% are UTC with a Z suffix (logging bug), so they look 5.5 hours earlier.
control (old checkout) or treatment (new one-page checkout).
Android mid/high, Android low-end, iOS or Web. Blank for about 1.0%.
1 if the user had never ordered before, else 0 (45% are new).
Tier 1, Tier 2 or Tier 3 city. Blank for about 2.9%.
organic, paid_social, paid_search, email, direct, or unknown (unknown is concentrated on Web: 23% of Web rows).
Orders placed in the 30 days before the test (0 for new users). Usable as a pre-experiment covariate.
Rupees spent in the 30 days before the test (0 for new users).
PRIMARY METRIC. 1 if the user completed a purchase during the test, else 0.
Rupees of revenue from the purchase (0 if not converted). Heavy right tail: 9 bulk orders above 100,000 rupees.
GUARDRAIL METRIC. 1 if the user hit a payment error, else 0.

gotchas: Sample-ratio mismatch: the test was meant to be 50/50 but control has 7,647 rows and treatment 6,701 (treatment share 46.7%, chi-square p = 2.8e-15). A redirect bug silently dropped low-end Android users from treatment (low-end Android is 19.3% of control but 10.0% of treatment), so the two arms are not comparable and the raw lift is biased upward.

Novelty effect: the observed lift is 4.5 percentage points in week 1 but only 1.4 percentage points and 1.4 percentage points in weeks 2 and 3. A single pooled number over 21 days overstates what will last.
Heavy-tailed revenue: 9 bulk orders above 100,000 rupees make up 59% of all revenue, so a mean-revenue t-test is unstable. Use medians, trimming, winsorising or a bootstrap.
Contaminated users and time zones: 170 users appear in both arms, and about 3.2% of timestamps are UTC instead of IST, which moves some assignments to the wrong day.

Missing and weak covariates: device_class is blank for about 1.0% and city_tier for about 2.9%, and the pre-period spend barely predicts conversion (correlation 0.05), so CUPED helps very little here.
tasks: Load the data, parse assign_ts (two formats), and count users per variant per day. Plot the daily split.
Test the 50/50 assignment with a chi-square (SRM) test. What does the p-value tell you, and should you trust the rest of the analysis yet?
Find the cause of the SRM: compare device_class, new_user and traffic_source mix between arms. Which segment is missing from treatment?
Compute the conversion lift with a two-proportion z-test and a 95% interval, first on all users, then after removing the segment that breaks the split from both arms. How much does the answer change?
Plot the lift by day or week and describe the shape. Decide what lift you would expect to keep after the novelty fades, and what you would report to the product manager.
Analyse revenue per user: show why the mean is unstable, then use a log transform, trimmed mean or bootstrap. Check the payment_error guardrail too.
Try variance reduction with pre_spend_30d (CUPED) and report how much the standard error shrinks, and why it is so small here.
Interview question: your A/B test shows a significant +3.5 point lift but the SRM check fails. Walk through what you do next and what you tell the stakeholder.
datasets.answer_key: SPOILER. Design: 15,000 users were randomised 50/50 (control or treatment). Treatment users on low-end Android were dropped with probability 0.55 by a redirect bug (822 users), so treatment has a richer device mix. Observed: control 14.5%, treatment 18.0% (lift 3.5 percentage points); SRM p = 2.8e-15. True effect of the new checkout (log-odds on conversion): +0.80 for new users and +0.25 for returning users on day 0, decaying as exp(-day/4), so it is about zero by day 14. In probability terms the true lift for users randomised to treatment was 3.2 percentage points in week 1, 0.5 percentage points in week 2 and 0.1 percentage points in week 3. Observed lift by week (all users): 4.5 percentage points, 1.4 percentage points, 1.4 percentage points; part of the later-week lift is the SRM selection bias, not the redesign. Revenue per converter is lognormal (median about 1,100 rupees) plus 9 bulk orders of 150,000 to 900,000 rupees (59% of revenue). Guardrail: payment_error is 4.4% in control and 5.4% in treatment (true +0.7 point harm). The right conclusion: do not ship on the pooled lift; fix the redirect bug, rerun, and expect a small long-run effect.
